rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command is to seize the condemned man and shackle him.
rows.anchor: Lay hold of him, and shackle him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After shackling him, the command is to make him enter hell.
rows.anchor: and then let him enter hell

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He is thrust into a chain of other sinners, seventy cubits long.
rows.anchor: the length whereof is seventy cubits

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: His punishment is tied to disbelief in God and lacking any urge to feed the needy.
rows.anchor: he did not believe in God, the Tremendous

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the afterlife he has no friend and no food except filth eaten by sinners.
rows.anchor: no friend has here today

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The shackles are allegorical; Asad directs readers to his notes on 13:5, 34:33, and 36:8.
rows.anchor: For an explanation of the allegory of "shackles"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Believers are urged to endure adversity with goodly patience.
rows.anchor: endure all advers ity with goodly patience

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People regard the reckoning as distant, while God sees it as near.
rows.anchor: look upon that [reckoning] as something far away

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Day is pictured with a sky like molten lead and mountains like tufts of wool.
rows.anchor: the sky will be like molten lead

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: No friend will ask about a friend on that Day, even though they can see one another.
rows.anchor: no friend will ask about his friend

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sinner would ransom himself with his children, spouse, brother, sheltering kin, and everyone else on earth.
rows.anchor: desire to ransom himself from suffering at the price of his own children

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The punishment awaiting the sinner is a raging flame.
rows.anchor: Verily, all [that awaits him] is a raging flame

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The flame tears away the sinner's skin.
rows.anchor: tearing away his skin

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The flame claims those who turn away from what is right and truth, hoard wealth, and withhold it from others.
rows.anchor: It will claim all such as turn their backs

words: قُلْ أُوحِىَ إِلَىَّ أَنَّهُ ٱسْتَمَعَ نَفَرٌۭ مِّنَ ٱلْجِنِّ فَقَالُوٓا۟ إِنَّا سَمِعْنَا قُرْءَانًا عَجَبًۭا
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The revelation reports that unseen beings listened and described the discourse as wondrous.
rows.anchor: some of the unseen beings gave ear

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They say the discourse guides toward right consciousness, and they believe in it.
rows.anchor: guiding towards consciousness of what is right; and so We have come to believe in it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The beings affirm God's exalted majesty and reject His having a consort or son.
rows.anchor: sublimely exalted is our Sustainer's majesty: no consort has He ever taken unto Himself, nor a son

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In context, istama'a means that the beings both heard and accepted the revelation.
rows.anchor: the meaning, in the above context, of the verbal form istama'a

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jinn has several Qur'anic connotations; here it may mean hitherto unseen beings or strangers.
rows.anchor: the jinn are referred to in the Qur'an in many connotations

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad tentatively reads these beings, as in 46:29–32, as strangers previously unseen by the people receiving the Qur'an.
rows.anchor: this expression may possibly signify

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: From 46:30 and their rejection of the Trinity at 72:3, Asad infers that they followed Mosaic faith and called the Qur'an a revelation after Moses, omitting Jesus.
rows.anchor: it transpires that the jinn in question were followers of the Mosaic faith

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad tentatively suggests they may have been Jews from Syria or Mesopotamia.
rows.anchor: they may have been Jews from distant parts of what is now the Arab world, perhaps from Syria or even Mesopotamia

rows.speaker: Tabari
rows.claim: Tabari says in several places that the jinn in this sūra and 46:29 onward came from Nasibin on the upper Euphrates.
rows.anchor: Tabari mentions in several places that the jinn referred to in this surah as well as in 46:29 ff. hailed from Nasibin

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: All worship belongs to God alone, so no one else is to be invoked alongside Him.
rows.anchor: all worship [14] is due to God [alone]: hence, do not invoke anyone side by side with God

words: وَأَنَّهُۥ لَمَّا قَامَ عَبْدُ ٱللَّهِ يَدْعُوهُ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Whenever God's servant stands in prayer, truth-deniers gather around and try to overwhelm him.
rows.anchor: whenever a servant of God stands up in prayer to Him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-masajid literally means places of worship, and here denotes worship as such.
rows.anchor: Lit, "the places of worship"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Libad, singular libdah, means that the crowds would almost be upon the servant.
rows.anchor: upon him in crowds (libad, sing. libdah

rows.speaker: Tabari
rows.claim: Tabari reads the crowding as an attempt to extinguish God's guiding light, alluding to 9:32.
rows.anchor: Tabari, evidently alluding to 9:32

words: وَأَنَّهُۥ لَمَّا قَامَ عَبْدُ ٱللَّهِ يَدْعُوهُ
rows.speaker: Most commentators
rows.claim: Most commentators take the initial reference to be Muhammad and the hostility of his pagan contemporaries.
rows.anchor: Most of the commentators assume that the above verse refers to the Prophet Muhammad and the hostility shown to him by his pagan contemporaries

words: وَأَنَّهُۥ لَمَّا قَامَ عَبْدُ ٱللَّهِ يَدْعُوهُ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad allows that initial setting but emphasizes a general pattern: majorities in every society oppose an individual or minority defending an evident but unpopular moral truth.
rows.anchor: the passage has a general import as well, alluding to the hostility shown by the majority of people, at all times and in all societies

words: وَأَنَّهُۥ لَمَّا قَامَ عَبْدُ ٱللَّهِ يَدْعُوهُ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad says the verse should be read with 19:73–74 and its notes.
rows.anchor: read in conjunction with 19:73-74 and the corresponding notes

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God says He created the man alone.
rows.anchor: him whom I have created alone

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God granted him vast resources.
rows.anchor: to whom I have granted resources vast

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God gave him children who are present as witnesses of his affection.
rows.anchor: and children as [love's ] witnesses

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God gave his life wide scope by endowing him with potentialities beyond those of other living beings.
rows.anchor: to whose life I gave so wide a scope

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Despite these gifts, the man greedily wants God to give him still more.
rows.anchor: he greedily desires that I give yet more

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wahid can mean either that God alone created the man or that God created the man alone.
rows.anchor: The above sentence can be understood in either of these two senses

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If wahid describes God, it stresses His uniqueness as Creator; if it describes the man, it evokes his utter loneliness at life's beginning and end.
rows.anchor: stressing His uniqueness as Creator - or to this particular object of His creation, man, who begins and ends his life in a state of utter loneliness

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Either reading emphasizes man's inescapable dependence on God.
rows.anchor: In either case, our attention is drawn to the fact of man's inescapable dependence on God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase also means to leave God alone to decide what to do with one who forgets his Creator and Sustainer, forbidding human punishment of truth-deniers.
rows.anchor: Leave it to Me alone to decide what to do with him who forgets that I am his Creator and Sustainer

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The expression means that God spread life wide for him, endowing him with potentialities beyond those of other living beings.
rows.anchor: whom I have endowed with potentialities far beyond those open to other living beings

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The man persistently and knowingly opposes God's messages.
rows.anchor: he knowingly, stubbornly sets himself

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God will constrain him to endure a painful uphill climb.
rows.anchor: I shall constrain him to endure a painful uphill climb

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On hearing the messages, he reflects on how to disprove them, destroys himself by that deliberation, looks for arguments, frowns, then turns away and glories in arrogance.
rows.anchor: he reflects and meditates [as to how to disprove them]

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He dismisses the revelation as old spellbinding eloquence and calls it the word of a mortal.
rows.anchor: handed down [from olden times]

rows.speaker: Lisan al-'Arab
rows.claim: Anid denotes someone who opposes or rejects something he knows to be true.
rows.anchor: denotes "one who opposes or rejects something that is true, knowing it to be true" (Lisan al-'Arab)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kana implies permanently recurring stubbornness despite its past-tense form; Asad therefore renders verses 18–25 in the present tense.
rows.anchor: the auxiliary verb kana, which indicates here a permanently recurring phenomenon despite its past-tense formulation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The denier calls the message nothing but the word of a mortal.
rows.anchor: This is nothing but the word of mortal man

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God will make him endure hell-fire in the life to come.
rows.anchor: I shall cause him to endure hell-fire

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hell neither allows life nor leaves the sufferer to die.
rows.anchor: It does not allow to live, and neither leaves

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rendering says hell makes truth visible to mortal man.
rows.anchor: making [all truth] visible to mortal man

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nineteen powers are set over hell.
rows.anchor: Over it are nineteen [powers]

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Saqar is the earliest Qur'anic occurrence of this term and one of seven metaphorical names for afterlife suffering, which man brings on himself through sin and deliberate blindness to spiritual truths.
rows.anchor: one of the seven metaphorical names given in the Qur'an to the concept of the suffering in the hereafter which man brings upon himself by sinning and deliberately remaining blind and deaf, in this world, to spiritual truths

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad reads this and Qur'anic descriptions of the hereafter allegorically, as the next verse and verses 28 onward indicate.
rows.anchor: The allegorical character of this and all other Qur'anic descriptions of man's condition and destiny in the hereafter is clearly alluded to in the subsequent verse

rows.speaker: Most commentators
rows.claim: Most commentators understand the phrase as changing or scorching human skin.
rows.anchor: Most of the commentators interpret the above elliptic phrase

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad follows the primary sense of laha, to appear, shine forth, or become visible, and takes lawwah as that which makes something visible.
rows.anchor: the rendering adopted by me, on the other hand, is based on the primary significance of the verb laha

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase describes the sinner's late recognition of truth, insight into his nature and past wrongs, and realization that he is responsible for his coming suffering.
rows.anchor: it relates to the sinner's belated cognition of the truth, as well as to his distressing insight into his own nature, his past failings

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sinner's state is neither life nor death, as also expressed at 87:12–13.
rows.anchor: a state neither of life nor of death

words: وَمَا جَعَلْنَآ أَصْحَٰبَ ٱلنَّارِ إِلَّا مَلَٰٓئِكَةًۭ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad renders the keepers over hell as angelic powers.
rows.anchor: For We have caused none but angelic powers to lord over the fire

words: وَمَا جَعَلْنَا عِدَّتَهُمْ إِلَّا فِتْنَةًۭ لِّلَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا۟
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their number is a trial for deniers, while it convinces earlier revelation recipients, strengthens believers, and frees both groups from doubt.
rows.anchor: their number to be aught but a trial for those who are bent on denying the truth

words: وَلِيَقُولَ ٱلَّذِينَ فِى قُلُوبِهِم مَّرَضٌۭ وَٱلْكَٰفِرُونَ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those with diseased hearts and outright deniers ask what God intends by the parable.
rows.anchor: they in whose hearts is disease

words: كَذَٰلِكَ يُضِلُّ ٱللَّهُ مَن يَشَآءُ وَيَهْدِى مَن يَشَآءُ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God lets astray those who will to go astray and guides those who will to be guided.
rows.anchor: In this way God lets go astray him that wills

words: وَمَا يَعْلَمُ جُنُودَ رَبِّكَ إِلَّا هُوَ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Only God comprehends the forces of the Sustainer.
rows.anchor: thy Sustaine rs forces save Him alone

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage is a reminder to mortal humanity.
rows.anchor: a reminder to mortal man

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Human conscious perception and conceptual thinking are called angelic powers because they enable discrimination between good and evil and spiritual ascent.
rows.anchor: by virtue of his powers of conscious perception and conceptual thinking that man can arrive at a discriminating cognition of good and evil

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because neglect or deliberate misuse of those powers causes sin and afterlife suffering, they are called lords of the fire; this complements “over it” in the preceding verse.
rows.anchor: a neglect or a deliberately wrong use of these angelic powers is at the root of all sinning on the part of man

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad takes the number as part of an allegory: deniers wrongly insist on literalizing it and so miss the passage's point.
rows.anchor: take the allegory in a literal sense, thus missing its point entirely

rows.speaker: Those who deny the truth
rows.claim: Deniers speculate about why Muhammad, whom they regard as the Qur'an's author, singled out one number.
rows.anchor: "those who are bent on denying the truth" are unwilling to recognize as such

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Understanding the allegory lets earlier revelation recipients recognize the Qur'an's rational approach to faith; this is the earliest statement of continuity in humanity's religious experience.
rows.anchor: the earliest statement outlining the principle of continuity in mankind's religious experience

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those with diseased hearts are half-hearted people able to discern right from wrong but inclined toward unbelief.
rows.anchor: the half-hearted ones who, despite their ability to discern between right and wrong, incline towards unbelief

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad notes the phrase also occurs at 2:26 and supplies “your” because unbelievers, rather than the Prophet, ask the question.
rows.anchor: the identical phrase in 2:26, together with the corresponding note 18

words: يُضِلُّ ٱللَّهُ مَن يَشَآءُ وَيَهْدِى مَن يَشَآءُ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad also allows “whomever He wills” as a rendering; the allegorical parable warns Qur'an followers against literal readings of eschatological descriptions.
rows.anchor: prevent the followers of the Qur'an from attaching a literal meaning to its eschatological descriptions

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closing reminder sentence makes explicit the parable's purpose, as at 2:26.
rows.anchor: a purpose that is unmistakably expressed in the concluding sentence of this passage

rows.speaker: Tabari, Zamakhshari, Baghawi, Ibn Kathir
rows.claim: These commentators take hiya as singular, referring to the feminine noun saqar, hell-fire.
rows.anchor: the feminine noun saqar, "hell-fire" (Tabari, Zamakhshari, Baghawi, Ibn Kathir)

rows.speaker: Razi
rows.claim: Razi takes hiya as plural, referring to the Qur'anic verses about these allegories.
rows.anchor: Razi pinpoints as "those [Qur'anic] verses dealing with these allegories

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad compromises between the readings with the rendering “all this.”
rows.anchor: my compromise rendering "all this"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because canonical salah was not yet obligatory when this early sūra was revealed, Asad takes prayer here broadly as conscious belief in God.
rows.anchor: this term is used in its widest sense, namely, conscious belief in God

words: لَا تُحَرِّكْ بِهِۦ لِسَانَكَ لِتَعْجَلَ بِهِۦٓ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is told not to hurry by repeating revelation with his tongue.
rows.anchor: MOVE NOT thy tongue in haste

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God undertakes to gather the revelation in the Prophet's heart and cause it to be read as it ought.
rows.anchor: it is for Us to gather it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When God recites it, the Prophet should follow its wording attentively.
rows.anchor: when We recite it, follow thou its wording

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God undertakes to make the revelation's meaning clear.
rows.anchor: it will be for Us to make its meaning clear

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most people love fleeting life and give no thought to the hereafter and Judgment Day.
rows.anchor: you love this fleeting life

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun refers to revelation's contents; the passage first addresses the Prophet, who feared forgetting words unless he repeated them as they came.
rows.anchor: the pronoun undoubtedly referring to the contents of revelation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage also applies to every believer who reads, listens to, or studies the Qur'an, and should be read with 20:114 and its note 101.
rows.anchor: both have also a wider import inasmuch as they apply to every believer who reads, listens to or studies the Qur'an

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: While 20:114 warns against hasty conclusions from isolated verses, this passage calls for patient study of the whole message and careful attention to every word and phrase.
rows.anchor: not to draw hasty - and therefore potentially erroneous - conclusions from isolated verses or statements of the Qur'an

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Readers and listeners should avoid mechanical fluency or delight in beautiful Qur'anic sound without understanding its message.
rows.anchor: remain satisfied with the mere beautiful sound of the Qur'anic language without understanding

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Gathering the revelation means causing the Prophet to remember it and read with mind and heart; it must be understood as one integrated whole, not as disconnected maxims, stories, or laws.
rows.anchor: make thee remember it and to cause it to be read with mind and heart

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Following the recitation means following the message as expressed in words; God attributes the recitation to Himself because He reveals the Qur'an and enables human understanding.
rows.anchor: follow thou its recitation

rows.speaker: Muhammad Abduh
rows.claim: Muhammad Abduh says that when the Qur'an is read as it ought to be, it becomes its own best commentary.
rows.anchor: Muhammad Abduh - "its own best commentary"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As the last breath reaches the throat, people ask whether a wizard can save the dying man.
rows.anchor: comes up to the throat

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The dying man knows this is parting and is wrapped in the pangs of death.
rows.anchor: knows that this is the parting

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At that point he feels impelled to turn toward his Sustainer.
rows.anchor: at that time towards thy Sustainer does he feel impelled to turn

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The driving toward the Sustainer is belated repentance.
rows.anchor: i.e., with belated repentance (see next three verses)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording rendered “at that time” literally reads “on that day”; the note breaks off while discussing yawm.
rows.anchor: "on that day"; but the term yawm is

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: His repentance is useless: while alive he did not accept truth or pray for enlightenment.
rows.anchor: he did not accept the truth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Instead, he denied the truth and turned away from it.
rows.anchor: he gave the lie to the truth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He then went arrogantly back to what he had come from.
rows.anchor: went arrogantly back to what he had come from

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage warns that man's end comes hourly nearer and nearer.
rows.anchor: and ever nearer unto thee, and nearer

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The interpolation that repentance is useless is needed to complete the sequence and rests on 4:17–18.
rows.anchor: based on 4:17-18, which has a definite bearing on the above passage

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad glosses “to his people” as the arrogant belief rooted in social materialism; the note breaks off mid-phrase.
rows.anchor: "to his people": i.e., to the arrogant belief, rooted in the materialism of his social
